time.desc: The leader of one party publicly accused his opponent of violating existing ceasefire arrangements and warned of possible consequences but did not clarify whether to suspend the upcoming contacts.

For the first time, a leader of one party publicly listed "promoting regime change of the opponent" as a foreign policy goal, accompanied by a tough threat on the nuclear issue, triggering a tough response from the opponent's senior leadership.

The two sides launched indirect negotiations at the technical level under the mediation of a third party. At the same time, the opponent simultaneously carried out live-fire military exercises and implemented short-term control of key sea lanes as a deterrent.
The mediator publicly stated that the two sides were close to reaching a nuclear and sanctions-related agreement, signaling a breakthrough in the negotiations.

The two countries and their allies launched large-scale joint air strikes against their opponents and escalated the confrontation into an open war. The first strike killed the opponent's top leader and triggered a reciprocal counterattack.

For the first time, the party that launched the air strike publicly admitted that the casualties in military operations were due to the opponent's drone strikes on its overseas/forward support points.
The opponent officially confirmed the change of the top leader and the successor took over the power, showing that the regime is still functioning after the "decapitation" blow.

The initiating party publicly issued a time-limited ultimatum, requiring the restoration of commercial navigation in key sea lanes, otherwise it will attack the opponent's key civilian infrastructure such as power supply.

The opponent's military stated that if the other party carried out attacks on energy facilities, it would completely close key sea lanes, and made countermeasures in response to tougher sanctions and threats of bombing.
The initiating party announced that it has opened dialogue and promised to suspend attacks on the opponent's energy facilities for a limited period, leaving a window for further diplomatic contacts.
The mobilizing party formally submitted a package of terms and plans to end the conflict to its opponents in an attempt to push the ceasefire arrangement into a textual negotiation stage.
The counterparty completed and formally submitted its response to the ceasefire terms plan, bringing the ceasefire negotiations into a new round-trip stage.
The two countries outside the region jointly proposed another multi-point plan to end the war, calling for an immediate ceasefire and the restoration of normal traffic on key sea lanes.
Leaders of the initiators made a national address, announcing a tougher crackdown in the coming weeks and setting a timetable for ending the operation as soon as possible.
The leaders of the initiating party agreed to suspend bombing of opponents and set a ceasefire window of about two weeks, and the market risk premium fell significantly.

One country's mainstream media revealed that its government is discussing plans to carry out military strikes on its opponent's nuclear facilities, and is evaluating expanding attacks by the end of the year to target its opponent's supreme leader.
The rival military launched a new missile offensive and fired missiles at an opponent's warship, while denying that it had closed the key strait.

For the first time, security figures from the ally of the party that launched the air strikes admitted that its air strikes lacked a feasible plan for regime change, and that the rival regime continued to exist after the attack on the leader.

The warring parties carried out air strikes on the air defense and naval facilities of the opponent's largest crude oil export hub. Multiple explosions were heard on the island, raising the risk of energy exports.

When the leader of one country was interviewed, he questioned the life and death of his opponent's new supreme leader and said that the opponent's agreement terms were not good enough. The opponent issued an open letter stating that he was willing to negotiate with mutual respect but would not give in.

A senior financial official of a country stated his position on shipping in the key strait and stated that he had no objection to the passage of ships from some countries, and for the first time linked energy mitigation measures to the duration of the conflict.
One of the opponent's highest-ranking officials (former speaker/secretary of an agency) was killed in an allied airstrike, becoming the highest-ranking official killed since the war began.
